title: The rain window
paragraphs: Rain began before the bakery opened, tracing thin lines down the glass.
I sat by the window with a cup that had already gone cold.
Across the street a cyclist waited under a narrow awning and laughed at the weather.
A bus arrived, paused, and left without taking anyone away.
By noon the clouds were tired and the street was full of reflected light.
I wrote three sentences in my notebook and crossed out only one.
When the rain stopped, the whole block smelled like stone and fresh bread.

title: The small library
paragraphs: The library on the corner opens early even on Saturdays.
I returned two books and chose a chair where the morning sun could reach the page.
Someone nearby turned a newspaper slowly, as if each page mattered.
The librarian stacked new arrivals without making a sound.
When the light moved across the table, I picked one more book and left.
A small bell rang behind me as the door closed.
At the end of the street I could still see the warm windows of the reading room.

title: The night train
paragraphs: The night train left the city with rain on its windows.
I watched the lights of small towns appear and disappear between fields.
A passenger across the aisle read a paper map and marked it with a pencil.
The conductor passed twice and each time the carriage grew quieter.
Somewhere after midnight the rain stopped and the sky opened.
I could see a single bright star above the dark line of the hills.
I kept that star in view until the train turned east toward morning.

title: Signals from the night sky
paragraphs: Most stars are too faint to see from a city street.
Light from buildings and cars makes the sky look emptier than it is.
To observe the night sky, find a place away from direct lamps.
Give your eyes time to adjust and keep your phone screen off.
A pair of binoculars can reveal craters on the moon and the moons of Jupiter.
Astronomers also study radio signals that human eyes cannot detect.
A large dish collects those waves and turns them into data.
Looking up is a practice in patience as much as a search for answers.

title: The last arcade
paragraphs: The arcade at the end of the street still opens after school.
Most machines are older than the students who play them.
A crowd gathers around the fighting game cabinet every Friday.
The owner keeps a notebook of high scores and repairs each stick by hand.
I learned to play there from someone who never told me their name.
We only spoke through the rhythm of buttons and the glow of the screen.
When the shutters come down, the alley keeps the sound of the last match.

title: The long way home
paragraphs: The road home began at the edge of a town I had never planned to visit.
I had missed the last bus by four minutes and the station clock refused to argue.
An old woman selling apples told me the next bus would come in the morning.
I bought two apples and asked whether there was a path along the river.
She pointed past the market and said the walk was longer but easier to remember.
I started walking while the sky was still bright enough to show the way.
The river moved beside the road with a sound like pages being turned.
Small houses stood behind fences, each with a garden and a chair facing the water.
A dog followed me for a hundred steps and then returned to its gate.
At the first bridge I stopped to read a sign about the town's old ferry.
The ferry had carried workers across the river before the bridge was built.
Now only a few posts remained in the water, dark and smooth with age.
I kept walking and the road slowly climbed away from the river.
Fields opened on both sides, and the wind carried the smell of cut grass.
A farmer on a tractor raised one hand as he passed.
I raised mine in return and felt oddly included in the evening.
The light turned gold, then orange, then a quiet blue.
I began to recognize the shape of the hills ahead and knew the town was close.
At a bend in the road I found a bench under a tree.
I sat down and ate the second apple while the first stars appeared.
A cyclist stopped to ask if I needed help and laughed when I said I was walking home.
He told me the road would join the highway in another hour.
I thanked him and chose the smaller lane behind the orchard instead.
The lane was darker, but it passed a house where someone was practicing the piano.
I walked slowly so the music would last a little longer.
The piano stopped, a door opened, and a cat stepped out into the road.
It looked at me once and disappeared between the trees.
Beyond the orchard the streetlights of my own town finally came into view.
They were not very bright, but they were the lights I knew.
I reached the front door long after dinner and long before midnight.
My shoes were dusty and my legs were tired.
Still, I stayed outside for a moment and listened to the night.
The long way home had given the day a better ending than the bus.
